title: Court pauses Big Bend border projects while legal challenge continues
summary:
A federal judge in Texas has temporarily blocked the Trump administration from building a border wall and related infrastructure across the Big Bend region. The ruling includes Big Bend National Park and a much larger stretch of the border with Mexico.

Judge Kathleen Cardone's Friday decision covers the roughly 500-mile Big Bend sector, about a quarter of the southern border with Mexico. The projects are part of a $46 billion administration effort involving steel walls, vehicle barriers, roads and surveillance technology.

The court order is a temporary injunction: in this case, a direction to stop construction while the legal dispute proceeds. Cardone said the people bringing the lawsuit were likely to succeed on at least one claim and could face serious harm that could not easily be undone without a pause. Her ruling does not settle the whole case.

An environmental organization, advocates for a historic church in Ruidosa and a river guide brought the lawsuit. They argue that the Department of Homeland Security acted wrongly by using waivers to bypass rules protecting the environment, culture and archaeology. A waiver sets aside a requirement that would otherwise apply.

Landowners, businesses and environmentalists have joined opposition to the projects. Critics say the region's remote location and rugged landscape already discourage unauthorized border crossings. Opposition to construction in the national park has included both Republicans and Democrats.

After bulldozers cleared land inside the park in August, Customs and Border Protection paused work there. That earlier pause expired on September 30. The administration says it is reevaluating its plans for the park, but has not announced what it will do.

The court's new ruling also covers areas upriver and downriver, where projects would largely cross private land. The government has sought landowners' permission to survey and build there.

Customs and Border Protection and the Department of Homeland Security did not immediately respond to requests for comment. Park advocates welcomed the ruling and urged officials to repair existing damage, meet local residents and develop alternative plans. For now, construction is paused while the legal challenge continues.
why_it_matters: The decision affects a national park and projects planned largely across private land nearby. It also raises a legal question about bypassing environmental and cultural protections.
